captions: Over the last six months, your feed was full
of it.

Screenshots of one lakh turning into forty-four.
Anonymous traders
posing with Lamborghinis.
Everyone, apparently, got rich.

So here's the honest question this video answers:
who
actually made money in the Indian market since the
spring — and how much of what you saw
was real?
We'll only use things we can verify — public

shareholding disclosures, exchange filings, and SEBI
orders. No invented
rags-to-riches.
Let's separate the winners from the fiction.
Here's the twist those viral posts hide.
The market didn't go up over these six months.
It fell — hard — and then clawed its
way back.
So the people who genuinely made money did it
against the tape, not with it.
That makes their methods worth studying — and it
makes the fakes much easier to spot, once you
know what you're looking at.
Look at the actual tape.
At the end of December, the Nifty fifty sat
near twenty-six thousand one hundred and thirty — an
all-time high.
Then it fell. By the second of April, it

had crashed to twenty-two thousand one hundred and
eighty-two

— down about sixteen percent in roughly three
months.
From there it recovered, and today it trades near

twenty-four thousand — still below where it began
the
year.
Read that again. Six months, and the index is
down.
So anyone who tells you this was an easy
market to get rich quick in is, at best,
forgetting — and at worst, selling you something.
Before we meet the winners, we need two questions.

They sound almost too simple. And almost nobody
actually
applies them.
Question one — is it verifiable?

A screenshot of a profit-and-loss screen proves
nothing; it
takes thirty seconds to fake.
But when an investor crosses one percent of a

listed company, the exchange forces them to disclose
it
— by law.

That paper trail — quarterly shareholding filings —
is
how we know what India's big investors truly own.
Not what they claim. What they filed.
Question two — over what time frame, and compared
to what?

Doubling your money sounds incredible — until you
learn
it took ten years, which is just seven percent
a year.

Or that the whole market doubled right alongside
you.
Every real number in this video comes with its
date and its benchmark.
Hold both questions in your head. They are the
difference between an investor and an audience.
Chapter two. The Retail King.
Our first verified winner made his fortune by doing
the opposite of everything the internet tells you.
He owns, essentially, one stock — and he almost
never talks about it.
Meet Radhakishan Damani.

By public filings, his disclosed equity is worth
around
one point nine eight lakh crore rupees — nearly
two trillion.
And here's the astonishing part: almost all of it
sits in a single company he founded and still
controls — Avenue Supermarts, the parent of DMart.
Sixty-seven percent of it.
The rest — VST Industries, a slice of three-M
India, a little United Breweries — barely moves the
needle.

Damani didn't spread himself across a hundred tips.
He
built one great business, and refused to sell it.
No interviews. No course. No channel. No calls.

Just decades of owning something excellent, and the
patience
to let it compound.
That patience is the entire strategy — and it's
the rarest thing on your feed.
Sit with that.
The richest retail investor in the country got there
slowly, in one business, in near-total silence.

The loudest voices online, meanwhile, are usually
selling access
to a secret they don't have.
Here's a rule of thumb worth keeping: the more

someone posts about their trades, the less you
should
trust their returns.
Chapter three. The SMILE investor.
If Damani is silence, our next winner is the

opposite — loud, joyful, and completely open about
how
he does it.
And his own life is the real version of
the rags-to-riches dream the fakes only imitate.

Vijay Kedia came to Mumbai around nineteen ninety
with
very little, after his family business faltered.
He learned the market the slow, painful way —

and built a disclosed portfolio worth roughly one
thousand

crore rupees today, across about twenty-one
companies.
His method even has a name — SMILE.

Small in size. Medium in experience. Large in
aspiration.
Extra-large in market potential.
In plain terms: he buys tiny companies with room
to become big ones — names like Tejas Networks,
Atul Auto, Cera Sanitaryware — and then he does
the hardest thing in investing.
He waits. Five years. Ten years.
Even now he's still adding — a fresh stake
in Eimco Elecon this June.
His edge isn't a secret indicator. It's conviction —
and a decade of holding through the noise.
Kedia likes to say the market rewards courage but
punishes greed.
Bulls make money. Bears make money. But pigs —
the greedy ones chasing every hot tip — get
slaughtered.
Every winner in this video, in their own way,
learned to sit still.
That's the muscle the fakes never show you building.
Chapter four. The Big Bull's legacy.

India's most famous investor, Rakesh Jhunjhunwala,
passed away in
twenty twenty-two.
But his portfolio didn't die with him — his
wife, Rekha, now stewards it. And over these six
months, it did something remarkable.

Rekha Jhunjhunwala's disclosed portfolio was worth
about forty-six thousand

nine hundred and eighty-two crore rupees on the
twenty-first
of July.

That's up nearly seven thousand seven hundred and
fifty

crore from thirty-nine thousand two hundred crore at
the
end of March.
Now hold that against our earlier chart.
While the index was still clawing back from its

April low, her book jumped almost twenty percent.
She
didn't just recover — she beat the market.
The engine, as ever, is Titan — a five-point-three

percent stake worth around twenty-two thousand
crore. Titan alone
made her richer by roughly three and a half
thousand crore since April.

The rest is classic Jhunjhunwala — Tata Motors,
Indian
Hotels, private banks.
And notice what she also did: she cut a

losing bet, slashing Star Health from about sixteen
percent
down to three.

Concentrated conviction, held for years, pruned when
a thesis
breaks. That is how you beat a flat market.
Stop and notice the pattern.
Three winners in, and not one of them made

their money day-trading, or chasing tips, or timing
the
market.
They own businesses. They wait.
Keep that in mind as the names get smaller
— because the method doesn't change.
Chapter five. The small-cap hunter.

Not every winner concentrates. Our next investor
does the

opposite — dozens of small, careful bets, letting
the
winners carry the pack.

Ashish Kacholia is one of India's most respected
small-cap
specialists.

His disclosed portfolio spans roughly forty-eight
companies — a

deliberately wide net across engineering, pharma,
and niche manufacturing.
And it worked, hard, this year: his disclosed book

jumped about forty-seven percent in a single quarter
—
from around two thousand two hundred crore in March
to over three thousand two hundred crore by June.

His largest bet, Shaily Engineering Plastics, is
worth over
seven hundred crore.
The philosophy is simple to say and brutally hard
to do.

Find small companies before the crowd. Do the
homework
nobody else will. Size each position so a single
mistake can't sink you.
Then let the two or three that truly work
compound into the bulk of your returns.

It's the venture-capital mindset, applied to listed
small-caps —
and you've never heard of most of his names.
That's exactly the point. He's early, not loud.
Here's something important.

Damani won by owning essentially one stock. Kacholia
won
by owning nearly fifty.
So which is correct?
Both.

Concentration and diversification are just two
honest answers to
risk. What they share is the discipline behind every
single position — and the patience to hold it.
That's the constant.
Chapter six. The diversifier.
If Kacholia casts a wide net, our next winner
casts the widest of all — and turns sheer
breadth into a strategy.

Mukul Agrawal runs one of the broadest star
portfolios

in India — around seventy-three disclosed companies,
worth roughly
six thousand four hundred crore rupees.
Where a beginner sees chaos, he sees risk control:
no single bet can wreck him, so he can

hold high-growth names through gut-wrenching
volatility.
His top positions read like a tour of new

India — Neuland Laboratories in pharma, Radico
Khaitan in
premium spirits, Nuvama in wealth management.

And crucially, he kept buying through this year's
turmoil

— adding Sudeep Pharma, Hindustan Construction, and
Sirca Paints
while others panicked.

Breadth, plus the nerve to keep deploying into
weakness.

That combination is why his hit-rate on multibaggers
is
among the best in the business.
Chapter seven. The quiet one.
The names so far command tens of thousands of
crores. Our next winner proves you can play this
game brilliantly with a fraction of that.
The name Dolly Khanna is famous in Indian markets
— though the portfolio is actually run by her
husband, Rajiv, and that's worth saying plainly.

Their disclosed book holds just about ten stocks,
worth
a little over two hundred crore rupees.

Tiny, by star-investor standards — and that's the
lesson.

They hunt unloved cyclical companies — chemicals,
metals, sugar,
textiles — and buy them before the market cares.
Prakash Industries. GHCL. SOM Distilleries.
Then they hold, quietly, for years, and sell into
strength when the crowd finally arrives.
Low turnover. High patience. No noise.
It's a reminder that the method scales down —
you don't need a fortune to invest like this.
You need temperament.
Let that sink in.

A ten-stock portfolio, run patiently, quietly, from
home —

outperformed the vast majority of loud, leveraged
'experts' online.
The edge was never the size of the account.
It was behaviour. And behaviour is the one thing
you can copy for free.
Chapter eight. The professional.
So far, individuals. Now the institutional mind — a
man who turned a repeatable process into a fund
empire.

Sunil Singhania is a chartered financial analyst who
founded
Abakkus Asset Management in twenty eighteen.

His personal disclosed book — around twenty-four
stocks, worth
roughly two thousand three hundred crore — is only
the visible tip; he manages far more for others.
What sets him apart isn't a hot tip. It's

a framework: durable earnings, sane valuations,
trustworthy management —

applied the same way, every time, across capital
goods,
consumer durables, and manufacturing.
Names like Carysil and Hindware.

The amateur chases the next big thing. The
professional
builds a process that survives being wrong — because

over enough decisions, repeatability beats
brilliance.

That's the quiet superpower the finfluencers can
never sell
you, because you can't fake a process.
Chapter nine. The sugar baron.
Our last individual winner made a fortune in the
least glamorous corner of the market — the one
everybody else scrolls past.
Anil Kumar Goel is known as the sugar baron
of Dalal Street.

His disclosed portfolio — around thirty-six stocks
worth close
to two thousand crore rupees — is a whole

book of 'boring' names: sugar, rice, paper,
packaging, textiles.

Triveni Engineering. Dalmia Bharat Sugar. K-R-B-L,
the basmati company.

Why boring? Because Goel understands operating
leverage.

Buy a cheap, out-of-favour cyclical near the bottom
of

its cycle, and when the upturn comes, profits
explode
— and so does the stock.
He holds for years and ignores the daily noise
completely.
There is no hot sector here, no story stock,

no hype. Just a deep understanding of unglamorous
businesses
— and the patience to wait for the cycle
to turn.

Nine verified winners. Loud and quiet, giant and
tiny,
concentrated and diversified.

And underneath, the same boring thread: own good
things,
and wait.
But you don't have to be a billionaire to
have made money these six months.
Let's look at how ordinary investors did it —
starting with where the money actually flowed.
Chapter ten. Where the money actually flowed.
In a market that fell and recovered, the gains

weren't spread evenly. One theme did the heavy
lifting.
As the market clawed back from its April low,
one sector led the charge — defence, and the
broader capital-expenditure story behind it.

Record government spending, a national push to build
weapons

at home instead of importing them, and multi-year
order

books turned companies like Bharat Electronics and
Hindustan Aeronautics
into the engines of the recovery.
Look at the gap.

From the April bottom, Bharat Electronics rebounded
about fifty-five
percent to record highs.
The defence sector as a whole was up roughly
twenty-four percent for the year.
The Nifty? Up about nine percent off the low.
Same six months, wildly different outcomes.
The people who made real money weren't smarter than
the index — they were simply standing where the
tailwind was blowing.
But here's the honesty most videos skip.
You're seeing this rally after it already happened.
A structural tailwind is real, but it is not
a promise — defence stocks have run hard, and

hot sectors are exactly where the next correction
tends
to start.

Recognising a trend is useful. Chasing it blindly,
at
the top, is how the fakes get their screenshots.
Chapter eleven. The IPO winners.
If any story fits 'made money in six months',

it's the new listings. A handful genuinely doubled.
But
the headline hides the truth.
The winners are real.

Omnitech Engineering, listed in March, is up over
one

hundred and fifty-eight percent from its issue
price.
SEDEMAC Mechatronics, up a hundred and twenty-six.
Shadowfax, up a hundred percent — a clean double.
Now look at the last bar.

The average listing gain across all thirty-two IPOs
this
year? Six-point-five percent.

For every headline double, there were many that
barely
moved — or fell.
And there's a catch even the average hides.
To make that money, you first had to be
allotted the shares — and popular IPOs are so

oversubscribed that most small applicants get
nothing at all.
So the viral 'I doubled my money on the

IPO' post is survivorship bias with an official
stamp:
you hear from the lucky few who got the
allotment and the pop — never from the thousands
who applied, got nothing, or bought a dud.

Real, but not repeatable-on-demand. Know the
difference.
Chapter twelve. The boring winners.
This is the most important chapter for most of
you — because it's the one strategy on this
list that anyone can actually copy.

There's a winner these six months who posted
nothing,
tipped nothing, and timed nothing.
The ordinary investor with a simple monthly S-I-P —
a systematic investment plan into mutual funds.
The most boring strategy in India.
And when the market crashed in April, it did
something the panicking traders couldn't.

In March, Indians poured a record thirty-two
thousand and
eighty-seven crore rupees into SIPs — in a single
month.

More than thirty-one thousand crore, every month,
for five
straight months.

Here's the magic: those SIP instalments kept buying
automatically,
on schedule, right through the April low.
No courage required. No forecast.

The plan bought the exact bottom that the
tip-chasers
were too scared to touch.
That's the whole trick of a SIP.
When prices fall, your fixed rupees simply buy more
units — so a crash lowers your average cost
instead of your resolve.

The volatility that terrified everyone else quietly
worked in
the SIP investor's favour.
They didn't beat the market with genius. They beat
it with a standing instruction — and the discipline
to leave it alone.
Chapter thirteen. Now the other half of the story
— the fakes.

Because while real investors were quietly
compounding, an entire

industry was manufacturing fake success. And the
regulator has
receipts.
Start with the biggest.

In December twenty twenty-five, SEBI came down on
Avadhut
Sathe and his trading academy.

Over eight years, they had collected around six
hundred
and one crore rupees from more than three lakh
people — under the banner of 'education'.

SEBI found it was really unregistered investment
advice, built
on showing off selective wins — and ordered five
hundred and forty-six crore disgorged.
Read that number again. That is the size of
the fake-success industry.

Then there's Asmita Patel, who branded herself the
she-wolf
of the stock market and the options queen.
SEBI barred her in February twenty twenty-five.

Her 'courses', the regulator said, were really
unregistered buy-and-sell
advice — and of roughly one hundred and four

crore rupees earned, more than fifty-three crore was
impounded.
The glamorous nickname wasn't a track record. It was
a marketing budget.
And the one that named the whole genre —
'Baap of Chart', the self-styled father of charts.

A huge following, a confident persona, and, SEBI
found,

unregistered advisory underneath — with seventeen
crore rupees ordered
disgorged back in twenty twenty-three.
Three names, one template.

Build an audience, promise the dream, sell the
course.

The trading profits were never the business. You
were.
Chapter fourteen. So how do you protect yourself?

Let's dissect the exact claim that probably brought
you
here — one lakh turned into forty-four — and
build a checklist you can use on any post,
forever.

Before the checklist, one number settles the whole
argument.

SEBI studied every individual trader in the futures
and
options market.

Ninety-three percent of them lost money — together,
more
than one point eight lakh crore rupees over three
years.
And losses got worse the next year, not better.

So when someone shows you one lakh becoming
forty-four,
remember: for every account like that — if it's
even real — there are roughly nine that quietly
blew up, and you will never see a single
one of them.
So here's your defence — six red flags.
One: no SEBI registration number — a real adviser
shows one; a finfluencer shows a lifestyle.

Two: screenshots instead of audited statements — one
takes
seconds to fake, the other doesn't.
Three: survivorship only — you see the win, never
the losses.

Four: the words 'guaranteed' or 'sure-shot' — an
instant
disqualifier.
Five: the course upsell — the real product is
the dream.
Six: a single lucky trade with no track record.
See two or more, and close the tab.
Chapter fifteen. Let's pull it together.

Across nine verified investors and every ordinary
winner, the

same handful of threads keep appearing. Copy these,
not
the screenshots.
Six threads.
One: quality first — own good businesses, or a
wide basket of them.
Two: time, not timing — hold for years.
Three: position sizing — never bet the farm on
one idea.

Four: no ruinous leverage — they compounded, they
didn't
gamble.
Five: they bought weakness — the crash was a
discount, not a disaster.
Six, and biggest: temperament.
Every real edge in this video was patience and
